concepts.name: Temperature
concepts.summary: Temperature tells us how hot or cold something is. We measure it with a thermometer.
concepts.learning_objective: Describe temperature as a measure of how hot or cold something is, measured with a thermometer in °C.
key_ideas: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius (°C).
Our sense of touch is not a reliable way to measure temperature.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, why touch cannot be trusted to judge temperature, and chooses a thermometer to measure it in °C.

concepts.name: Heat Energy
concepts.summary: Heat is energy. Temperature tells us how hot something is; heat is the energy that can flow.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that heat is a form of energy and that heat and temperature are different.
key_ideas: Heat is a form of energy.
A big pot of warm water can hold more heat than a cup of hotter water.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, for two amounts of material at the same temperature, that the larger amount holds more heat energy, so it can melt more ice or stay warm for longer.

concepts.name: Heat Flow
concepts.summary: Heat always flows from hotter to colder, until both are the same temperature.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that heat flows from a hotter object or region to a colder one until they reach the same temperature.
key_ideas: Heat moves from a hotter place to a colder place.
Heat flow stops when both objects reach the same temperature.
"Cold" is not something that flows — only heat flows.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that heat flows from the hotter object to the colder one until both reach the same temperature, without describing cold as something that flows.

concepts.name: Heat Conduction
concepts.summary: Good conductors like metal let heat pass through them quickly.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that metals conduct heat faster than wood or plastic, so they draw heat from our hands faster and feel colder.
key_ideas: Metals are good conductors of heat.
A good conductor takes heat away from your hand faster, so it feels colder.
Two objects in the same room are at the same temperature.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that a metal object feels colder because it conducts heat away from the hand faster, not because it is at a lower temperature.

concepts.name: Heat Insulators
concepts.summary: Insulators slow down the flow of heat. They keep hot things hot and cold things cold.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that poor conductors (insulators) such as wood, plastic, air and cloth slow down heat flow.
key_ideas: Wood, plastic, cloth, and trapped air are poor conductors of heat.
Insulators slow heat flow in BOTH directions — in and out.
A jacket does not make heat; it slows heat leaving your body.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that an insulator such as cloth, foam or trapped air slows down heat flow in either direction and does not produce heat itself.

concepts.name: Expansion & Contraction
concepts.summary: When things gain heat they expand (get bigger). When they lose heat they contract.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that most materials expand when they gain heat and contract when they lose heat.
key_ideas: Solids, liquids and gases expand when heated.
Gaps are left in railway tracks so they can expand on hot days.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that a material expands when it gains heat and contracts when it loses heat, and uses this to account for what is observed.

misconceptions.label: Metal is colder
misconceptions.statement: Metal is naturally colder than other materials.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Both objects are at room temperature; metal feels colder because it conducts heat away from your hand faster.

misconceptions.label: Cold flows
misconceptions.statement: Cold flows from cold objects into warm objects.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Only heat flows, and it flows from hotter to colder. Things cool down because they lose heat.

misconceptions.label: Clothes make heat
misconceptions.statement: A jacket or blanket produces its own heat.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Insulators do not produce heat; they slow down heat loss from your body.

misconceptions.label: Heat vs Temperature
misconceptions.statement: Heat and temperature are the same thing.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Temperature measures how hot something is; heat is energy that flows. A bigger amount of material can hold more heat at the same temperature.

forces.name: Forces
forces.subject: Primary Science
forces.tagline: What makes things move, stop, or change shape?
forces.description: Discover pushes and pulls all around you — gravity, friction, magnets and springs — and find out why a moving ball does not need a push to keep going.
forces.syllabus_ref: MOE Primary Science Syllabus (2023) · Interactions · Forces (approximate mapping, pending teacher review)

concepts.name: What Is a Force?
concepts.summary: A force is a push or a pull. We cannot see forces, but we can see what they do.
concepts.learning_objective: Describe a force as a push or a pull, and recognise that forces can act by contact or at a distance.
key_ideas: A force is a push or a pull.
Some forces need contact (friction, a kick); some act at a distance (gravity, magnetic force).
concepts.mastery_criterion: Identifies, in a new everyday situation, the push or pull acting on an object and explains whether it needs contact (like friction) or acts at a distance (like gravity or magnetic force).

concepts.name: Forces & Motion
concepts.summary: Forces change how things move. A moving object keeps moving unless a force like friction slows it down.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that a force can make an object start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, change direction or change shape.
key_ideas: Forces can change an object's speed, direction of motion or shape.
A moving object does NOT need a continuous push to keep moving.
Moving things slow down and stop because forces such as friction act against them.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that a moving object keeps moving without a continuous push and slows down or stops because forces such as friction act against it.

concepts.name: Magnetic Force
concepts.summary: Magnets pull on magnetic materials like iron and steel — even without touching them.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that magnets attract only magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt, and that the force can act at a distance.
key_ideas: Magnets attract magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt.
Not all metals are magnetic — aluminium and copper are not.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Predicts, for a new set of objects, which ones a magnet attracts, and explains that only magnetic materials such as iron and steel are attracted, not all metals.

concepts.name: Elastic Spring Force
concepts.summary: When you stretch or squash a spring, it pushes or pulls back to get its shape back.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that a stretched or compressed spring or rubber band exerts an elastic spring force as it tries to return to its original shape.
key_ideas: A stretched or squashed spring exerts an elastic spring force.
The more a spring is stretched or squashed, the bigger the elastic spring force.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that a stretched or squashed spring or rubber band exerts an elastic spring force as it returns to its original shape, and that more stretch gives a bigger force.

concepts.name: Gravity
concepts.summary: Gravity pulls everything towards the Earth. Heavy and light objects fall at the same rate when air resistance is small.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that gravity is a pull of the Earth on all objects, and that without air resistance objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass.
key_ideas: Gravity is a non-contact force that pulls objects towards the Earth.
A heavier object does not fall faster when air resistance is very small.
Air resistance slows down light, wide objects like feathers and paper.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Predicts, for two objects of different mass dropped together in a new setting, that they land at about the same time when air resistance is small, and explains this using gravity.

concepts.name: Friction
concepts.summary: Friction acts when two surfaces rub. It slows things down — and it also helps us walk, grip and brake.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact, and that it can be both useful and a problem.
key_ideas: Friction opposes motion between two surfaces in contact.
Rough surfaces give more friction; smooth surfaces give less.
Friction is useful for walking, gripping and braking, but it also causes wear and heat.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, how more or less friction helps or hinders, showing that friction can be useful (gripping, braking) and is not always a problem.

concepts.name: Weight & Mass
concepts.summary: Mass is how much matter something has. Weight is how hard gravity pulls on it.
concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish mass (amount of matter, in kg) from weight (the pull of gravity on an object, in newtons).
key_ideas: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg).
Weight is the force of gravity on an object, measured in newtons (N).
On the Moon your mass stays the same, but your weight is less.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, for an object taken to a place with weaker or stronger gravity, that its mass stays the same while its weight changes.

misconceptions.label: Force vs Motion
misconceptions.statement: A moving object needs a continuous force to keep moving, and it stops when the force "runs out".
misconceptions.corrective_target: A moving object keeps moving unless a force acts on it. It slows down and stops because friction (and air resistance) act against its motion.

misconceptions.label: Heavier falls faster
misconceptions.statement: Heavier objects always fall faster than lighter objects.
misconceptions.corrective_target: When air resistance is very small, gravity makes heavy and light objects fall at the same rate, so they land at the same time.

misconceptions.label: Friction always bad
misconceptions.statement: Friction is always bad and we should get rid of it.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Friction can be useful — it lets tyres and shoes grip the ground and lets brakes stop a bicycle. It is only a problem in some situations.

misconceptions.label: Magnets and metals
misconceptions.statement: Magnets attract all metals.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Magnets only attract magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Many metals, like aluminium and copper, are not magnetic.

misconceptions.label: Mass vs Weight
misconceptions.statement: Mass and weight are the same thing, so an object's mass changes when gravity changes.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the pull of gravity, so it changes when gravity is weaker or stronger.

misconceptions.label: Forces need touching
misconceptions.statement: A force can only act when two objects are touching.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Some forces, such as gravity and magnetic force, act without touching. They are non-contact forces that act at a distance.

matter.name: Matter
matter.subject: Primary Science
matter.tagline: What is everything made of — and how does it change?
matter.description: Explore solids, liquids and gases, find out why air has mass, and discover what really happens when water melts, boils, evaporates and condenses.
matter.syllabus_ref: MOE Primary Science Syllabus (2023) · Cycles · Matter and changes of state; states of matter also draw on Diversity (approximate mapping, pending teacher review)

concepts.name: States of Matter
concepts.summary: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. It can be a solid, a liquid or a gas.
concepts.learning_objective: Describe matter as anything that has mass and occupies space, existing as solid, liquid or gas.
key_ideas: Matter has mass and takes up space.
The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Classifies a new everyday item as a solid, liquid or gas, and justifies that it is matter because it has mass and takes up space.

concepts.name: Solids, Liquids & Gases
concepts.summary: Solids keep their shape. Liquids keep their volume but take the shape of the container. Gases fill any space.
concepts.learning_objective: Compare solids, liquids and gases in terms of definite shape, definite volume and whether they can be compressed.
key_ideas: Solids have a definite shape and a definite volume.
Liquids have a definite volume but no definite shape.
Gases have no definite shape and no definite volume, and can be compressed.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, which properties (shape, volume, whether it can be compressed) change and which stay the same for a solid, a liquid or a gas.

concepts.name: Air Has Mass
concepts.summary: Air may be invisible, but it has mass and takes up space, just like solids and liquids.
concepts.learning_objective: Show that air is matter — it has mass and takes up space.
key_ideas: Air has mass, so a ball pumped with more air is slightly heavier.
Air takes up space — that is why an "empty" cup pushed upside down into water stays dry inside.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that air and other gases have mass and take up space, so adding or removing gas changes the mass.

concepts.name: Melting & Freezing

Freezing is a liquid changing into a solid when it loses heat.
Pure water melts and freezes at 0°C.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that a solid melts when it gains heat and a liquid freezes when it loses heat, without describing cold as something that goes in or out.

concepts.name: Evaporation & Boiling
concepts.summary: Water can evaporate at any temperature. Boiling is fast evaporation at 100°C, with bubbles of water vapour.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that evaporation turns liquid water into water vapour at any temperature, while boiling happens quickly at 100°C with bubbles of water vapour.
key_ideas: Evaporation happens at the surface of a liquid at any temperature.
Heat, wind, and a larger exposed surface make evaporation faster.
The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, not air.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that water evaporates into water vapour at any temperature, and that the bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, not air.

concepts.name: Dissolving vs Melting

Melting involves one substance changing state because it gains heat.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Decides, in a new everyday situation, whether a substance is dissolving or melting, and gives evidence (such as taste, or what is left after evaporation) that a dissolved substance is still there.

concepts.name: Condensation
concepts.summary: When water vapour touches something cold, it loses heat and turns back into tiny water droplets.
concepts.learning_objective: Explain that water vapour in the air condenses into water droplets when it loses heat to a cooler surface.
key_ideas: Air contains water vapour, especially in humid Singapore.
Water vapour loses heat to a cool surface and condenses into water droplets.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that droplets on a cold surface come from water vapour in the air that loses heat and condenses, not from liquid leaking through.

misconceptions.label: Air has no mass
misconceptions.statement: Air has no mass because it is invisible and feels like nothing.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Air is matter. It has mass and takes up space, so adding air to a ball makes it slightly heavier.

misconceptions.label: Melting vs Dissolving
misconceptions.statement: Sugar or salt "melts" when it disappears in water.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Sugar dissolves — it spreads out in the liquid and is still there. Melting is a solid turning into a liquid when it gains heat.

misconceptions.label: Evaporation needs boiling
misconceptions.statement: Water can only turn into water vapour when it boils at 100°C.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Evaporation happens at any temperature, slowly, from the surface of the water. Boiling is just fast evaporation at 100°C.

misconceptions.label: Bubbles are air
misconceptions.statement: The bubbles in boiling water are air.
misconceptions.corrective_target: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour — liquid water that has changed into a gas and rises out of the water.

misconceptions.label: Droplets leak through glass
misconceptions.statement: The water droplets on the outside of a cold glass come from the drink leaking through the glass.
misconceptions.corrective_target: The droplets come from water vapour in the surrounding air, which loses heat to the cold glass and condenses.

misconceptions.label: Cold goes in or out

misconceptions.corrective_target: Only heat moves. A liquid freezes when it loses heat, and a solid melts when it gains heat.

concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, why touch cannot be trusted to judge temperature, and chooses a thermometer to measure it in °C.

concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, for two amounts of material at the same temperature, that the larger amount holds more heat energy, so it can melt more ice or stay warm for longer.

"Cold" is not something that flows — only heat flows.
concepts.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that heat flows from the hotter object to the colder one until both reach the same temperature, without describing cold as something that flows.

questions.prompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been in the same room overnight. Why does the metal spoon feel colder when you touch it?
hints: Think about what your hand is doing when you touch the spoon.
Do objects in the same room end up at different temperatures?

demo_answers.misconception: Because metal is colder than wood. Metal naturally has a lower temperature.
demo_answers.dialogue: Maybe the metal takes heat from my hand faster.
demo_answers.correct: Both spoons are at room temperature, but metal is a good conductor so it takes heat away from my hand faster.

questions.prompt: Mei puts ice cubes into a glass of warm orange juice. After a few minutes the juice is cooler. Explain what happened.
hints: Which is hotter at the start — the juice or the ice?
Heat always flows from ... to ...?

demo_answers.misconception: The ice gives out cold to the juice so the juice becomes cold.
demo_answers.dialogue: The juice loses heat to the ice.
demo_answers.correct: Heat flows from the warmer juice into the colder ice, so the juice loses heat and the ice melts.

questions.prompt: On a cold day, Ravi wears a thick woollen sweater and feels warm. Explain how the sweater keeps him warm.
hints: Where does the heat come from in the first place — the sweater or Ravi?

demo_answers.misconception: The sweater makes heat so Ravi feels warm.
demo_answers.dialogue: The sweater slows down the heat leaving his body.
demo_answers.correct: Wool is a poor conductor of heat, so it slows down heat loss from Ravi's body.

questions.prompt: A bathtub of water and a small cup of water are both at 40°C. Which one can melt more ice cubes? Explain.
hints: Temperature is the same. What else could be different?

demo_answers.misconception: They can melt the same amount because heat is the same as temperature.
demo_answers.dialogue: The bathtub has more water so it has more heat.
demo_answers.correct: The bathtub, because it has more water so it holds more heat energy even at the same temperature.

questions.prompt: Why are small gaps left between sections of railway tracks?
hints: What happens to metal on a very hot day?

demo_answers.misconception: So that water can drain away.
demo_answers.dialogue: The tracks expand when they get hot.
demo_answers.correct: When the tracks gain heat on a hot day they expand, so the gaps give them room and they won't bend.

questions.prompt: Siti dips one hand in cold water and the other in warm water. Then she puts both hands in room-temperature water. Why do her hands feel different, and how could she find the real temperature?
hints: What tool do scientists use to measure temperature?

demo_answers.misconception: The water is different temperatures in different places.
demo_answers.dialogue: She should use a thermometer.
demo_answers.correct: Her hands were at different temperatures before so touch is not reliable. She should use a thermometer.

questions.prompt: Ali wraps one ice cube in a woollen cloth and leaves another ice cube unwrapped on the table. His friend says, "The wrapped one will melt first, because wool is warm." Which ice cube melts first? Explain.
hints: Does wool make heat, or does it only slow heat down?
Where does the heat that melts the ice come from?

demo_answers.misconception: The wrapped ice cube melts first because the wool cloth makes heat and warms it up.
demo_answers.dialogue: The wool slows down heat from the warm air getting into the ice.
demo_answers.correct: The unwrapped ice cube melts first. Wool is a poor conductor of heat, so it slows down heat flowing from the warm air into the wrapped ice cube.

questions.prompt: A bottle of milk is too hot for baby Aisha. Mum stands the bottle in a basin of cool tap water. Explain what happens to the milk and the water. When does this stop?
hints: Which is hotter at the start — the milk or the water?
Will the milk keep cooling forever, or does it stop at some point?

demo_answers.misconception: The cool water gives cold to the milk until the milk becomes cold.
demo_answers.dialogue: The milk loses heat to the water until they are the same temperature.
demo_answers.correct: Heat flows from the hotter milk into the cooler water, so the milk loses heat and the water gains heat. This stops when both reach the same temperature.

questions.prompt: Ravi kicks a football across the school field. After it leaves his foot, the ball keeps rolling, then slows down and stops. Why does the ball stop?
hints: Is Ravi's foot still touching the ball while it rolls?
What is rubbing against the ball as it rolls on the grass?

demo_answers.misconception: The ball stops because the force from Ravi's kick runs out. It needs a force to keep moving.
demo_answers.dialogue: Friction from the grass slows the ball down until it stops.
demo_answers.correct: After the kick, the ball keeps rolling on its own. Friction between the ball and the grass acts against its motion and slows it down until it stops.

questions.prompt: From the second-floor corridor, Ahmad drops a heavy metal ball and a lighter wooden ball of the same size at the same time. Which ball reaches the ground first? Explain.
hints: Gravity pulls on both balls. Does being heavier really make a ball fall faster?
Both balls are the same size and shape. Is air resistance very different for them?

demo_answers.misconception: The metal ball lands first because heavier things fall faster.
demo_answers.dialogue: Oh, they land at the same time because air resistance is tiny for both balls.
demo_answers.correct: Both balls land at about the same time. Gravity pulls both down and they fall at the same rate, even though one is heavier.

questions.prompt: Ravi's friend says: "Friction is always bad. Bicycle tyres should be totally smooth!" Ravi disagrees. Why do bicycle tyres have grooves on them?
hints: What would happen if Ravi rode on a wet road with totally smooth tyres?
Do grooves make the tyre surface rougher or smoother?

demo_answers.misconception: I agree with the friend. Friction is always bad because it slows the bicycle down, so smooth tyres are better.
demo_answers.dialogue: Maybe we need friction so the tyres grip the road and don't slip.
demo_answers.correct: I disagree. The grooves increase friction between the tyres and the road, so the tyres grip the road and do not slip, especially when braking.

questions.prompt: Siti holds a magnet near four objects — a steel paper clip, an aluminium drink can, a copper wire and an iron nail. Which objects will the magnet attract? Explain.
hints: Is every metal a magnetic material?
Which of the four objects are made of iron or steel?

demo_answers.misconception: All four, because magnets attract all metals.
demo_answers.dialogue: Oh, only some metals are magnetic, like iron and steel.
demo_answers.correct: Only the steel paper clip and the iron nail are attracted. Magnets only attract magnetic materials like iron and steel. Aluminium and copper are metals, but they are not magnetic.

questions.prompt: Mei pulls back the rubber band on a toy launcher and lets go. Her paper plane shoots forward. What made the plane move? What would happen if she stretched the rubber band further?
hints: What does a stretched rubber band try to do when you let go?
Does a rubber band pull back harder when it is stretched a lot or a little?

demo_answers.misconception: The plane moves because Mei's hand threw it.
demo_answers.dialogue: The rubber band pulls back to its original shape and pushes the plane.
demo_answers.correct: The stretched rubber band exerts an elastic spring force as it goes back to its original shape, and this pushes the plane forward. If she stretches it further, the elastic force is bigger, so the plane flies further.

questions.prompt: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. He travels to the Moon, where gravity is weaker. What happens to his mass and his weight on the Moon?
hints: Does the astronaut lose any part of his body on the way to the Moon?
Weight is the pull of gravity. What happens to the pull on the Moon?

demo_answers.misconception: His mass becomes less on the Moon because weight and mass are the same thing.
demo_answers.dialogue: His mass stays the same because he still has the same amount of matter. Only his weight changes.
demo_answers.correct: His mass stays the same at 60 kg, but his weight is less because the Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's.

questions.prompt: A ripe mango drops from a tree in Siti's garden. Nothing touches the mango as it falls. Is there a force acting on the mango? Explain.
hints: What made the mango start moving down?
Can a magnet pull a paper clip without touching it?

demo_answers.misconception: No, there is no force on the mango because nothing is touching it.
demo_answers.dialogue: Oh, gravity is pulling the mango down even without touching it.
demo_answers.correct: Yes. Gravity is pulling the mango down towards the Earth. Gravity is a non-contact force, so it can act without touching the mango.

questions.prompt: Ravi's bicycle brakes squeak. His friend says: "Friction is bad. Just put oil on the brake pads so they rub less." Is this a good idea? Explain.
hints: How do brake pads make a wheel slow down?
What would oil do to the friction between the pads and the wheel?

demo_answers.misconception: Yes, friction is always bad, so oiling the brake pads will make the bicycle better.
demo_answers.dialogue: The brakes need friction to slow the wheel down, so oil is a bad idea.
demo_answers.correct: No, it is not a good idea. The brakes need friction between the brake pads and the wheel to slow the bicycle down and stop it. Oil would reduce the friction, so Ravi might not be able to stop safely.

questions.prompt: Ravi weighs a flat basketball on an electronic balance. Then he pumps it full of air and weighs it again. What happens to the reading? Explain.
hints: Is air matter? What do all kinds of matter have?
What did Ravi add to the ball?

demo_answers.misconception: The reading stays the same because air has no mass.
demo_answers.dialogue: Oh, the air pumped in has mass, so the ball becomes a bit heavier.
demo_answers.correct: The reading increases a little. Air has mass, so pumping more air into the ball makes it heavier.

questions.prompt: Siti pours 250 ml of orange juice from a tall glass into a wide, flat bowl. Does the shape of the juice change? Does its volume change? Explain.
hints: Did Siti spill or add any juice?
Does a liquid keep its own shape, or take the shape of what it's in?

demo_answers.misconception: There is less juice now because it looks lower in the bowl.
demo_answers.dialogue: The volume is the same, only the shape changed.
demo_answers.correct: The juice takes the shape of the bowl, so its shape changes. But its volume stays the same at 250 ml because liquids have a definite volume.

questions.prompt: Mei stirs a spoonful of sugar into her hot kopi. After a while, she cannot see the sugar anymore. Her brother says the sugar melted. Is he right? Explain.
hints: Does the kopi taste sweet after the sugar disappears?
Would sugar also disappear in cold water?

demo_answers.misconception: Yes, the sugar melted in the hot kopi because the kopi is hot.
demo_answers.dialogue: Oh, the sugar dissolved in the kopi and it is still there, that's why it tastes sweet.
demo_answers.correct: No. The sugar dissolved in the kopi. It spread out into tiny bits in the liquid, so it is still there and the kopi tastes sweet.

questions.prompt: Siti's mother hangs wet clothes on the bamboo poles outside their HDB flat on a sunny morning. By afternoon, the clothes are dry, but the water never got anywhere near 100°C. Where did the water go?
hints: Does water need to boil before it can turn into water vapour?
Where does a puddle go on a sunny day?

demo_answers.misconception: The sun made the water very hot until it reached 100°C, so it boiled away.
demo_answers.dialogue: Maybe water can evaporate slowly at room temperature, even without boiling.
demo_answers.correct: The water evaporated. It slowly changed into water vapour and went into the surrounding air. Evaporation can happen at any temperature, and the sun and wind make it faster.

questions.prompt: Ravi watches a pot of water boiling on the stove. Big bubbles form at the bottom and rise to the top. What is inside the bubbles?
hints: The pot only has water in it. What can water change into when it gets very hot?
What happens to the water level if you keep boiling it?

demo_answers.misconception: The bubbles are air that was trapped in the water.
demo_answers.dialogue: So the bubbles are water that turned into water vapour.
demo_answers.correct: The bubbles are water vapour. When the water boils, it gains heat and changes into a gas inside the pot, and the bubbles rise and escape into the air.

questions.prompt: At the hawker centre, Ahmad orders a glass of iced Milo. After a few minutes, tiny water droplets appear on the outside of the glass. Where do the droplets come from?
hints: Is there water in the air around us, even if we can't see it?
What happens to water vapour when it touches something cold?

demo_answers.misconception: The Milo leaks through the glass and comes out on the outside.
demo_answers.dialogue: Maybe the water comes from water vapour in the air around the glass.
demo_answers.correct: Water vapour in the warm surrounding air touches the cold glass. It loses heat and condenses into water droplets on the outside of the glass.

questions.prompt: Siti pours orange juice into ice-pop moulds and puts them in the freezer. The next morning, the juice has become hard ice pops. Explain what happened to the juice.
hints: Is the freezer colder or warmer than the juice?
Which way does heat flow between the juice and the freezer?

demo_answers.misconception: The cold from the freezer went into the juice and made it hard.
demo_answers.dialogue: The juice lost heat to the colder freezer, so it froze.
demo_answers.correct: The juice lost heat to the colder air in the freezer. It froze and changed from a liquid into a solid.

questions.prompt: Ravi keeps a chocolate bar in his shorts pocket during a sunny PE lesson. Later, the chocolate is soft and sticky. Explain what happened to the chocolate.
hints: In the hot sun, is the chocolate gaining heat or losing heat?
What do we call it when a solid changes into a liquid?

demo_answers.misconception: The chocolate became soft because it lost its coldness in the sun.
demo_answers.dialogue: The chocolate gained heat from the sun and his body, so it melted.
demo_answers.correct: The chocolate gained heat from the hot sun and from Ravi's warm body, so it melted and changed from a solid into a liquid.

pathways.expected_explanation: Only the steel paper clip and the iron nail, because magnets only attract magnetic materials like iron and steel. Aluminium and copper are metals but are not magnetic.
reasoning_points: The steel paper clip and the iron nail are attracted.
Not all metals are magnetic — aluminium and copper are not attracted.
Magnets only attract magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt).
required_points: The steel paper clip and the iron nail are attracted.
Not all metals are magnetic — aluminium and copper are not attracted.

misconceptions.label: Magnets and metals
misconceptions.statement: Magnets attract all metals.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Magnets only attract magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt. Many metals, like aluminium and copper, are not magnetic.

hints: Is every metal a magnetic material?
Which of the four objects are made of iron or steel?

transfer_questions.prompt: At a recycling centre, a big magnet is used to separate steel cans from aluminium cans. Why does this work?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The magnet attracts the steel cans because steel is a magnetic material. Aluminium is not magnetic, so the aluminium cans are left behind.
reasoning: Steel is a magnetic material, so the magnet attracts the steel cans.
Aluminium is not magnetic, so aluminium cans are not attracted.

transfer_questions.prompt: A fridge magnet sticks to the steel door of Siti's fridge, but it will not stick to the aluminium window frame. Both are metals. Why is there a difference?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Steel is a magnetic material, so the magnet is attracted to the fridge door. Aluminium is a metal but it is not magnetic, so the magnet does not stick to the window frame.
reasoning: Steel is a magnetic material, so the magnet is attracted to it.
Aluminium is not magnetic, so the magnet does not stick to it.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Predicts, for a new set of objects, which ones a magnet attracts, and explains that only magnetic materials such as iron and steel are attracted, not all metals.

pathways.learning_objective: Explain that a stretched or compressed spring or rubber band exerts an elastic spring force as it tries to return to its original shape.
pathways.diagnostic_question: Mei pulls back the rubber band on a toy launcher and lets go. Her paper plane shoots forward. What made the plane move? What would happen if she stretched the rubber band further?
pathways.expected_explanation: The stretched rubber band exerts an elastic spring force as it returns to its original shape, pushing the plane forward. Stretching it further gives a bigger elastic force, so the plane flies further.
reasoning_points: The stretched rubber band exerts an elastic spring force as it returns to its original shape.
Stretching it more gives a bigger force, so the plane goes further.
required_points: The stretched rubber band exerts an elastic spring force as it returns to its original shape.
Stretching it more gives a bigger force, so the plane goes further.
hints: What does a stretched rubber band try to do when you let go?
Does a rubber band pull back harder when it is stretched a lot or a little?

transfer_questions.prompt: Ravi's bicycle seat has springs under it. When he sits down, the springs get shorter. When he gets off, they become longer again. Explain why.
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Ravi's weight squashes the springs. The squashed springs exert an elastic spring force that pushes back, so when he gets off they return to their original shape.
reasoning: The squashed springs exert an elastic spring force and return to their original shape.

transfer_questions.prompt: When Ahmad lands on a trampoline, the springs around the edge stretch. Then he is pushed up into the air. What pushes him up? What happens if he lands harder?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The stretched springs exert an elastic spring force as they return to their original shape, which pushes Ahmad up. Landing harder stretches the springs more, so the elastic spring force is bigger and he goes higher.
reasoning: The stretched springs exert an elastic spring force as they return to their original shape.
More stretch gives a bigger force, so he goes higher.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that a stretched or squashed spring or rubber band exerts an elastic spring force as it returns to its original shape, and that more stretch gives a bigger force.

pathways.learning_objective: Distinguish mass (amount of matter, in kg) from weight (the pull of gravity on an object, in newtons).
pathways.diagnostic_question: An astronaut has a mass of 60 kg on Earth. He travels to the Moon, where gravity is weaker. What happens to his mass and his weight on the Moon?
pathways.expected_explanation: His mass stays the same at 60 kg because the amount of matter does not change, but his weight is less because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
reasoning_points: His mass stays the same (60 kg).
His weight is less because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
The Moon's weaker gravity causes the lower weight.
required_points: His mass stays the same (60 kg).
His weight is less because the Moon's gravity is weaker.
The Moon's weaker gravity causes the lower weight.

misconceptions.label: Mass vs Weight
misconceptions.statement: Mass and weight are the same thing, so an object's mass changes when gravity changes.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Mass is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere. Weight is the pull of gravity, so it changes when gravity is weaker or stronger.

hints: Does the astronaut lose any part of his body on the way to the Moon?
Weight is the pull of gravity. What happens to the pull on the Moon?

transfer_questions.prompt: An astronaut brings a 2 kg rock from the Moon back to Earth. Does its mass change? Is its weight on Earth more or less than on the Moon?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Its mass stays the same at 2 kg, but its weight is greater on Earth because Earth's gravity is stronger.
reasoning: The rock's mass stays the same (2 kg).
Its weight is greater on Earth because Earth's gravity is stronger.
Earth's stronger gravity causes the greater weight.

transfer_questions.prompt: Gravity on Mars is weaker than on Earth. A robot rover has a mass of 900 kg on Earth. What happens to its mass and its weight when it lands on Mars?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Its mass stays the same at 900 kg because the amount of matter does not change, but its weight is less because the gravity on Mars is weaker.
reasoning: The rover's mass stays the same (900 kg).
Its weight is less because gravity on Mars is weaker.
Mars's weaker gravity causes the lower weight.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, for an object taken to a place with weaker or stronger gravity, that its mass stays the same while its weight changes.

pathways.learning_objective: Describe a force as a push or a pull, and recognise that forces can act by contact or at a distance.
pathways.diagnostic_question: A ripe mango drops from a tree in Siti's garden. Nothing touches the mango as it falls. Is there a force acting on the mango? Explain.
pathways.expected_explanation: Yes. Gravity, the pull of the Earth, acts on the mango and pulls it down. Gravity is a non-contact force, so it can act without touching the mango.
reasoning_points: The force is gravity — the pull of the Earth on the mango.
Gravity acts without touching — it is a non-contact force.
required_points: The force is gravity — the pull of the Earth on the mango.
Gravity acts without touching — it is a non-contact force.

misconceptions.label: Forces need touching
misconceptions.statement: A force can only act when two objects are touching.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Some forces, such as gravity and magnetic force, act without touching. They are non-contact forces that act at a distance.

hints: What made the mango start moving down?
Can a magnet pull a paper clip without touching it?

transfer_questions.prompt: Ravi holds a magnet a few centimetres above a steel paper clip. The clip jumps up and sticks to the magnet. Did a force act on the clip before it touched the magnet? Explain.
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Yes. The magnetic force pulled the clip up before it touched the magnet. Magnetic force is a non-contact force, so it acts at a distance.
reasoning: The magnet pulled (attracted) the clip.
Magnetic force acts without touching — it is a non-contact force.

transfer_questions.prompt: During PE, Ahmad throws a ball straight up. After it leaves his hand, nothing touches it, but it slows down, stops and comes back down. Which force does this? Does it need to touch the ball?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Gravity. It pulls the ball towards the Earth without touching it, because gravity is a non-contact force.
reasoning: Gravity pulls the ball back towards the Earth.
Gravity acts without touching — it is a non-contact force.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Identifies, in a new everyday situation, the push or pull acting on an object and explains whether it needs contact (like friction) or acts at a distance (like gravity or magnetic force).

pathways.learning_objective: Explain that friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact, and that it can be both useful and a problem.
pathways.diagnostic_question: Ravi's bicycle brakes squeak. His friend says: "Friction is bad. Just put oil on the brake pads so they rub less." Is this a good idea? Explain.
pathways.expected_explanation: No. The brakes need friction between the brake pads and the wheel to slow the bicycle down and stop it. Oil would reduce the friction, so Ravi might not be able to stop safely. Here, friction is useful.
reasoning_points: The brakes work by friction between the pads and the wheel, which slows the bicycle down.
Oil reduces friction, so the bicycle cannot stop well.
required_points: The brakes work by friction between the pads and the wheel, which slows the bicycle down.

misconceptions.label: Friction always bad
misconceptions.statement: Friction is always bad and we should get rid of it.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Friction can be useful — it lets tyres and shoes grip the ground and lets brakes stop a bicycle. It is only a problem in some situations.

hints: How do brake pads make a wheel slow down?
What would oil do to the friction between the pads and the wheel?

transfer_questions.prompt: Mei's friend wants to polish the school hall floor until it is super smooth, so that everyone can run faster. Why could this be dangerous?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: A very smooth floor has less friction, so shoes cannot grip the floor and people may slip and fall. Friction is useful for walking and running.
reasoning: Less friction means shoes cannot grip, so people slip.

transfer_questions.prompt: A goalkeeper wears gloves with rough rubber palms. How do these gloves help him catch and hold a wet football?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The rough rubber palms increase friction between the gloves and the ball, so he can grip the wet ball and it does not slip out of his hands.
reasoning: The rough palms increase friction so he can grip the ball without it slipping.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, how more or less friction helps or hinders, showing that friction can be useful (gripping, braking) and is not always a problem.

pathways.learning_objective: Show that air is matter — it has mass and takes up space.
pathways.diagnostic_question: Ravi weighs a flat basketball on an electronic balance. Then he pumps it full of air and weighs it again. What happens to the reading? Explain.
pathways.expected_explanation: The reading increases slightly, because air has mass. Pumping more air into the ball adds mass.
reasoning_points: The reading (mass) increases slightly.
Air has mass.
required_points: Air has mass.

misconceptions.label: Air has no mass
misconceptions.statement: Air has no mass because it is invisible and feels like nothing.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Air is matter. It has mass and takes up space, so adding air to a ball makes it slightly heavier.

hints: Is air matter? What do all kinds of matter have?
What did Ravi add to the ball?

transfer_questions.prompt: Mei hangs two blown-up balloons at the two ends of a ruler so that it balances. She pops one balloon. Which side of the ruler goes up? Why?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The side with the popped balloon goes up, because the air that escaped had mass, so that side became lighter.
reasoning: The escaped air had mass, so that side became lighter.

transfer_questions.prompt: Ahmad weighs a closed bottle of fizzy drink. He opens it, lets the fizzy gas escape, closes it again and weighs it once more. Is the bottle lighter or heavier now? Why?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: It is slightly lighter, because the gas that escaped had mass.
reasoning: The escaped gas had mass, so the bottle lost mass.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that air and other gases have mass and take up space, so adding or removing gas changes the mass.

pathways.learning_objective: Compare solids, liquids and gases in terms of definite shape, definite volume and whether they can be compressed.
pathways.diagnostic_question: Siti pours 250 ml of orange juice from a tall glass into a wide, flat bowl. Does the shape of the juice change? Does its volume change? Explain.
pathways.expected_explanation: The shape changes because a liquid takes the shape of its container, but the volume stays the same at 250 ml because a liquid has a definite volume.
reasoning_points: The juice takes the shape of the bowl — liquids have no definite shape.
The volume stays the same — liquids have a definite volume.
required_points: The juice takes the shape of the bowl — liquids have no definite shape.
The volume stays the same — liquids have a definite volume.
hints: Did Siti spill or add any juice?
Does a liquid keep its own shape, or take the shape of what it's in?

transfer_questions.prompt: Ahmad seals the tip of a syringe full of air and pushes the plunger. It moves in a little. Would the same thing happen if the syringe were full of water? Explain.
transfer_questions.expected_answer: No. Air is a gas with no definite volume, so it can be compressed. Water is a liquid with a definite volume, so it cannot be compressed much.
reasoning: Air (gas) can be compressed but water (liquid) has a definite volume and cannot.

transfer_questions.prompt: Ravi moves a wooden block from a small box into a big basket. Does the block's shape or volume change? Explain.
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Neither changes. A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume, so the block keeps its own shape and volume in any container.
reasoning: A solid has a definite shape and a definite volume.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, which properties (shape, volume, whether it can be compressed) change and which stay the same for a solid, a liquid or a gas.

pathways.learning_objective: Distinguish dissolving (a substance mixing evenly into a liquid) from melting (a solid turning into a liquid when it gains heat).
pathways.diagnostic_question: Mei stirs a spoonful of sugar into her hot kopi. After a while, she cannot see the sugar anymore. Her brother says the sugar melted. Is he right? Explain.
pathways.expected_explanation: No. The sugar dissolved — it spread out in the kopi and is still there, which is why the kopi tastes sweet. Melting needs heat to turn a solid into a liquid on its own.
reasoning_points: The sugar dissolved in the kopi.
The sugar is still there — the kopi tastes sweet.
required_points: The sugar dissolved in the kopi.

misconceptions.label: Melting vs Dissolving
misconceptions.statement: Sugar or salt "melts" when it disappears in water.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Sugar dissolves — it spreads out in the liquid and is still there. Melting is a solid turning into a liquid when it gains heat.

hints: Does the kopi taste sweet after the sugar disappears?
Would sugar also disappear in cold water?

transfer_questions.prompt: Ahmad stirs a spoonful of salt into a glass of room-temperature water. The salt disappears from view. Is this melting or dissolving? How could he show the salt is still there?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: It is dissolving. The salt is still in the water — he could taste it, or let the water evaporate and the salt would be left behind.
reasoning: The salt dissolved.
The salt is still there and can be shown by tasting or evaporating the water.

transfer_questions.prompt: Siti puts a piece of butter into a hot pan, and a spoonful of salt into a pot of soup. Both seem to disappear. Which one melted and which one dissolved? Explain.
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The butter melted — it gained heat from the hot pan and changed from a solid into a liquid. The salt dissolved — it spread out in the soup and is still there, so the soup tastes salty.
reasoning: The butter melted because it gained heat.
The salt dissolved in the soup and is still there.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Decides, in a new everyday situation, whether a substance is dissolving or melting, and gives evidence (such as taste, or what is left after evaporation) that a dissolved substance is still there.

pathways.learning_objective: Explain that evaporation turns liquid water into water vapour at any temperature, while boiling happens quickly at 100°C with bubbles of water vapour.
pathways.diagnostic_question: Siti's mother hangs wet clothes on the bamboo poles outside their HDB flat on a sunny morning. By afternoon, the clothes are dry, but the water never got anywhere near 100°C. Where did the water go?
pathways.expected_explanation: The water evaporated — it slowly changed into water vapour and went into the surrounding air. Evaporation can happen at any temperature; the sun and wind make it faster.
reasoning_points: The water evaporated.
It became water vapour in the surrounding air.
Evaporation happens at any temperature (no boiling needed).
required_points: The water evaporated.
It became water vapour in the surrounding air.

misconceptions.label: Evaporation needs boiling
misconceptions.statement: Water can only turn into water vapour when it boils at 100°C.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Evaporation happens at any temperature, slowly, from the surface of the water. Boiling is just fast evaporation at 100°C.

hints: Does water need to boil before it can turn into water vapour?
Where does a puddle go on a sunny day?

transfer_questions.prompt: After a rainy morning, there is a puddle on the school field. By the end of recess, the puddle is gone. What happened to the water?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The water in the puddle evaporated into water vapour in the air.
reasoning: The water evaporated.

transfer_questions.prompt: Mum mops the kitchen floor in the morning. Twenty minutes later the floor is dry, even though nobody heated it. Where did the water go? Why does turning on the fan make it dry faster?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The water evaporated into water vapour in the air, even at room temperature. The wind from the fan makes evaporation faster.
reasoning: The water evaporated.
Moving air from the fan makes evaporation faster.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that water evaporates into water vapour at any temperature, and that the bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, not air.

pathways.learning_objective: Explain that evaporation turns liquid water into water vapour at any temperature, while boiling happens quickly at 100°C with bubbles of water vapour.
pathways.diagnostic_question: Ravi watches a pot of water boiling on the stove. Big bubbles form at the bottom and rise to the top. What is inside the bubbles?
pathways.expected_explanation: The bubbles are water vapour. The water gains heat, changes into a gas inside the pot, and the bubbles rise and escape into the air.
reasoning_points: The bubbles are water vapour (water that has changed into a gas).
The water gains heat and boils.
required_points: The bubbles are water vapour (water that has changed into a gas).

misconceptions.label: Bubbles are air
misconceptions.statement: The bubbles in boiling water are air.
misconceptions.corrective_target: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapour — liquid water that has changed into a gas and rises out of the water.

hints: The pot only has water in it. What can water change into when it gets very hot?
What happens to the water level if you keep boiling it?

transfer_questions.prompt: Mei boils water in a glass kettle and forgets to switch it off. The water level goes down, and bubbles keep forming. Where did the missing water go?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The water changed into water vapour in the bubbles and escaped into the air, so the water level dropped.
reasoning: The water changed into water vapour and escaped.

transfer_questions.prompt: Ravi watches instant noodles cooking in a pot of boiling water. Big bubbles keep rising from the bottom, and the water level slowly drops. What is inside the bubbles, and where does the missing water go?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The bubbles are water vapour. The water gains heat, changes into a gas and escapes into the air, so the water level drops.
reasoning: The bubbles are water vapour, which escapes into the air.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that water evaporates into water vapour at any temperature, and that the bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, not air.

pathways.learning_objective: Explain that water vapour in the air condenses into water droplets when it loses heat to a cooler surface.
pathways.diagnostic_question: At the hawker centre, Ahmad orders a glass of iced Milo. After a few minutes, tiny water droplets appear on the outside of the glass. Where do the droplets come from?
pathways.expected_explanation: Water vapour in the warm surrounding air touches the cold glass, loses heat and condenses into water droplets on the outside of the glass.
reasoning_points: The water comes from water vapour in the surrounding air.
The water vapour loses heat to the cold glass and condenses.
required_points: The water comes from water vapour in the surrounding air.
The water vapour loses heat to the cold glass and condenses.

misconceptions.label: Droplets leak through glass
misconceptions.statement: The water droplets on the outside of a cold glass come from the drink leaking through the glass.
misconceptions.corrective_target: The droplets come from water vapour in the surrounding air, which loses heat to the cold glass and condenses.

hints: Is there water in the air around us, even if we can't see it?
What happens to water vapour when it touches something cold?

transfer_questions.prompt: Ravi's family drives with the air-con on. On a humid morning, tiny water droplets appear on the OUTSIDE of the car windows. Explain why.
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The warm air outside contains water vapour. It touches the cold window, loses heat and condenses into water droplets.
reasoning: The outside air contains water vapour.
The water vapour loses heat to the cold window and condenses.

transfer_questions.prompt: Siti takes a can of cold 100PLUS out of the fridge. Soon the outside of the can is wet, even though the can is still sealed. Where did the water come from?
transfer_questions.expected_answer: Water vapour in the air lost heat to the cold can and condensed into water droplets on its surface.
reasoning: The water came from water vapour in the air.
The water vapour lost heat to the cold can and condensed.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that droplets on a cold surface come from water vapour in the air that loses heat and condenses, not from liquid leaking through.

pathways.learning_objective: Explain that a solid melts when it gains heat and a liquid freezes (solidifies) when it loses heat.
pathways.diagnostic_question: Siti pours orange juice into ice-pop moulds and puts them in the freezer. The next morning, the juice has become hard ice pops. Explain what happened to the juice.
pathways.expected_explanation: The juice lost heat to the colder air in the freezer. When it lost enough heat, it froze — it changed from a liquid into a solid.
reasoning_points: The juice loses heat to the colder freezer.
The juice freezes — it changes from a liquid into a solid.
required_points: The juice loses heat to the colder freezer.
The juice freezes — it changes from a liquid into a solid.

misconceptions.label: Cold goes in or out
misconceptions.statement: Things freeze because cold goes into them, and melt because their cold leaves them.
misconceptions.corrective_target: Only heat moves. A liquid freezes when it loses heat, and a solid melts when it gains heat.

hints: Is the freezer colder or warmer than the juice?
Which way does heat flow between the juice and the freezer?

transfer_questions.prompt: Ahmad fills an ice-cube tray with water and puts it in the freezer. Explain how the water becomes ice.
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The water loses heat to the colder air in the freezer, so it freezes and changes from a liquid into solid ice.
reasoning: The water loses heat to the colder freezer.

transfer_questions.prompt: At a factory, workers pour hot liquid metal into moulds. As it cools, the metal becomes solid. Explain what happens to the metal, using the idea of heat.
transfer_questions.expected_answer: The liquid metal loses heat to the cooler mould and air, so it changes from a liquid into a solid, even though it is still hot.
reasoning: The liquid metal loses heat to its cooler surroundings.

pathways.mastery_criterion: Explains, in a new everyday situation, that a solid melts when it gains heat and a liquid freezes when it loses heat, without describing cold as something that goes in or out.

transfer_questions.expected_answer: The wax near the flame gains heat from the flame, so it melts and changes from a solid into a liquid.
reasoning: The wax gains heat from the flame.
